paragraphs.text: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is the most common systemic autoimmune disease. It affects about 1% of the adult population worldwide and has an estimated heritability of 60% (Begovich et al., 2004). Barton et al. (2001) described RA as an oligogenic autoimmune disease. paragraphs.text: Hasstedt et al. (1994) performed likelihood analysis of 28 pedigrees ascertained through pairs of first-degree relatives with RA, assuming tight linkage to HLA. Their results supported an HLA-linked RA susceptibility locus with an allele frequency of 2.16% and a lifetime penetrance of 41% in male homozygotes and 48% in female homozygotes. Inheritance was recessive in males and nearly recessive in females. Of the variance within genotypes, 78% was attributable to genetic or environmental effects shared by sibs. The inferred HLA-linked locus accounted for about one-half of familial RA but only about one-fifth of RA in the population, and the authors suggested that a large portion of RA cases may occur sporadically.

paragraphs.text: Cornélis et al. (1998) performed a genome scan in 114 European Caucasian RA sib pairs from 97 nuclear families. Linkage was significant only for HLA (P less than 2.5 x 10(-5)). They then studied candidate regions at 18q22-q23 (D18S68-D18S61-D18S469) and 3q13 (D3S1267) in 194 additional RA sib pairs from 164 nuclear families. Support for linkage was extended only for chromosome 3 (P = 0.002). Analysis of all 261 families gave P = 0.001 and suggested an interaction between this putative RA locus and HLA. The authors estimated that the locus could account for 16% of the genetic component of RA and suggested CD80 and CD86 as candidate genes.

paragraphs.text: Jawaheer et al. Stratification into white or seropositive subgroups revealed some additional markers with improved significance. Several nominally significant regions overlapped loci previously implicated in RA or in other autoimmune diseases, including systemic lupus erythematosus (D1S235), inflammatory bowel disease (D4S1647, D5S1462, D16S516), multiple sclerosis (D12S1052), and ankylosing spondylitis (D16S516). paragraphs.text: Sigurdsson et al. (2007) analyzed 5 SNPs in IRF5 and 3 SNPs in TYK2 in a Swedish cohort of 1,530 RA patients and 881 controls. Four of the 5 SNPs in the 5-prime region of IRF5 were associated with RA, whereas none of the TYK2 SNPs were. The minor alleles of 3 IRF5 SNPs were in linkage disequilibrium and formed a relatively common haplotype (frequency about 0.33) that appeared to protect against RA. The association was seen mainly in anti-CCP-negative patients, and a suggestive association with anti-CCP-negative RA was also seen in a Dutch replication cohort of 387 patients and 181 controls.

paragraphs.text: In a genomewide association study, Plenge et al. (2007) genotyped 317,503 SNPs in 1,522 anti-CCP-positive RA cases and 1,850 matched controls from the NARAC and Swedish EIRA cohorts. A SNP on chromosome 9, rs3761847, was associated with RA in all samples tested, including an independent replication set (odds ratio, 1.32; 95% CI, 1.23-1.42; P = 4 x 10(-14)). Because rs3761847 is in linkage disequilibrium with TRAF1 and C5, 2 genes relevant to chronic inflammation, the authors concluded that a common variant at the TRAF1-C5 locus is associated with an increased risk of anti-CCP-positive RA. The study also confirmed associations with the MHC and PTPN22.

paragraphs.text: Remmers et al. (2007) tested SNPs in and around 13 candidate genes in the previously linked region of chromosome 2q in 1,620 North American patients with established RA and 2,635 controls, and fine-mapped the STAT1-STAT4 region. A SNP haplotype in the third intron of STAT4 was associated with susceptibility to RA. The minor alleles of the haplotype-defining SNPs were present on 27% of chromosomes from patients and 22% from controls (for rs7574865, P = 2.81 x 10(-7); odds ratio, 1.32). The association was replicated in 1,529 Swedish patients with early RA and 881 controls (P = 0.02). Homozygosity for the risk allele, compared with absence of the allele, was associated with a 60% increased risk of RA.

paragraphs.text: Thomson et al. (2007) genotyped 10 SNPs, 9 of which were newly suggested by the WTCCC genome-wide association screen, in an independent UK cohort of 5,063 RA cases and 3,849 controls. They replicated the association of rs6920220 (G-A) at 6q23 (minor-allele odds ratio, 1.23; trend P = 1.1 x 10(-8)); in the combined WTCCC and validation data the odds ratio was 1.22 (trend P = 3.6 x 10(-12)). rs6920220 lay in an intergenic linkage disequilibrium block of about 60 kb that contained no known genes but included part of a PTPN11 pseudogene and lay between OLIG3 and TNFAIP3. The authors noted that TNFAIP3, a negative regulator of NF-kappa-B, was a plausible candidate because TNFAIP3-deficient mice develop multiorgan inflammation that includes the joints. They found no evidence of interaction between rs6920220 and the HLA-DRB1 or PTPN22 susceptibility markers. Together, the HLA-DRB1 shared epitope, PTPN22 rs2476601, and rs6920220 accounted for 8.5% of the total variance in RA susceptibility. They confirmed the PTPN22 rs2476601 association (odds ratio, 1.53; trend P = 2.0 x 10(-18)), found only modest evidence for rs743777 in IL2RB (combined trend P = 5.3 x 10(-6)) and borderline evidence for rs11761231 near PODXL (trend P = 0.042), and found no association with rs2104286 in IL2RA.

paragraphs.text: In a separate study, Plenge et al. (2007) genotyped 116,204 SNPs in 397 individuals with RA and compared them with 1,211 related individuals from the Framingham Heart Study. The association was reproducible in 5,541 additional case-control samples (P = 10(-3) in the GWA scan, P less than 10(-6) in replication, and P = 10(-9) combined). rs10499194 and rs6920220, which lies 3.8 kb away and had been reported by the WTCCC, were statistically independent. Each association was reproducible when their data were compared with the WTCCC data, and together the 2 SNPs defined risk and protective haplotypes for RA at 6q23.

The authors concluded that STAT4 is emerging as a common risk factor for diverse complex diseases.

paragraphs.text: Raychaudhuri et al. (2008) combined 2 published GWA studies of European RA in a meta-analysis (3,393 cases and 12,462 controls) and tested 31 top-ranked SNPs in a replication set of 3,929 autoantibody-positive cases and 5,807 matched controls from 8 collections. A common variant at the CD40 locus on chromosome 20q13, rs4810485, reached P = 8.2 x 10(-9) overall (odds ratio, 0.87). This SNP lies in the second intron of CD40 and is in near-perfect linkage disequilibrium (r2 = 0.95) with rs1883832, a variant that disrupts a Kozak sequence and has been shown to affect the efficiency of CD40 protein translation. The authors concluded that this pointed to a putative functional variant and supported a central role for the CD40 signaling pathway in autoantibody-positive RA. They also found association at the CCL21 locus on 9p13 (rs2812378; replication P = 0.00097, overall P = 2.8 x 10(-7)); this SNP lies about 0.1 kb from the CCL21 5-prime UTR in an LD block that contains the CCL21 coding sequence. Evidence of association at 4 more loci, MMEL1-TNFRSF14 (rs3890745, overall P = 1.1 x 10(-7)), CDK6 (rs42041, P = 4.0 x 10(-6)), PRKCQ (rs4750316, P = 4.4 x 10(-6)), and KIF5A-PIP4K2C (rs1678542, P = 8.8 x 10(-8)), still needed further validation. The meta-analysis confirmed associations at PTPN22, 6q23 (TNFAIP3), STAT4, and TRAF1-C5, and association was also observed at 4q27 (IL2/IL21) and CTLA4 but not at PADI4.

paragraphs.text: Barton et al. (2009) genotyped 18 SNPs from 14 putative type 1 diabetes susceptibility loci in 3,962 UK RA cases and 3,531 controls and found a new RA susceptibility locus at AFF3. In a combined analysis of 6,819 RA cases and 12,650 controls, rs10865035 was associated with RA (odds ratio, 1.12; 95% CI, 1.07-1.17; P = 2.8 x 10(-7)). The associated variants mapped to the 5-prime and promoter region of AFF3, which is preferentially expressed in lymphoid cells and encodes a nuclear factor with transcriptional activation domains. They replicated the association of RA with the CTLA4 SNP rs3087243 (odds ratio, 0.87; P = 1.1 x 10(-4)), which was confirmed in a meta-analysis with 2 earlier well-powered studies (odds ratio, 0.88; P = 2.6 x 10(-6)), and with rs6822844 in the IL2-IL21 region on 4q27, where the common allele predisposed to disease (odds ratio, 0.86; P = 5.4 x 10(-4)). The common allele of the IL7R SNP rs6897932 showed a trend toward association (odds ratio, 0.90; P = 0.007) that did not reach their corrected significance threshold.

paragraphs.text: Orozco et al. (2009) fine-mapped 70 SNPs at 6q23 in 3,962 UK RA patients and 3,531 controls and found 18 SNPs associated with RA. The strongest association was with rs6920220 (P = 2.6 x 10(-6); odds ratio, 1.22). The next strongest was with rs13207033 (P = 0.0001; odds ratio, 0.86), which was perfectly correlated with rs10499194; the authors described this as the first independent replication of that SNP. In conditional logistic regression, 3 SNPs stayed significant: rs6920220, rs13207033 (protective), and rs5029937 in intron 2 of TNFAIP3 (191163). Carrying the risk alleles of both rs6920220 and rs5029937 without the protective allele of rs13207033 gave an odds ratio of 1.86 compared with carrying none, equivalent to an effect size of 1.50 compared with controls. The authors noted that the rs5029937 effect needed replication in an independent cohort.

paragraphs.text: In a genome-wide association study of 2,418 RA cases and 4,504 controls from North America, Gregersen et al. (2009) identified an association at the REL locus on chromosome 2p13 (rs13031237, P = 6.01 x 10(-10)), the second most significant non-MHC association after PTPN22. They replicated the association in 2,604 cases and 2,882 controls; in the combined dataset the allelic odds ratio was 1.25 (P = 3.08 x 10(-14)) for rs13031237 and 1.21 (P = 2.60 x 10(-11)) for rs13017599. The scan confirmed the strongest association in the MHC region (P = 9.50 x 10(-104)) and the associations at PTPN22 (rs2476601, P = 1.62 x 10(-21)) and the TRAF1/C5 region (rs881375, P = 4.09 x 10(-8)). The combined dataset gave definitive support for associations with CTLA4 (rs231735; odds ratio, 0.85; P = 6.25 x 10(-9)) and BLK (rs2736340; odds ratio, 1.19; P = 5.69 x 10(-9)). Genotype-specific results showed codominance at all loci except CTLA4, which was nearly dominant, and no significant gene-gene interactions were found after correction for multiple testing.

paragraphs.text: Raychaudhuri et al. (2009) used GRAIL, a text-mining method, to score 179 loci with P less than 0.001 in a published RA GWAS meta-analysis (3,393 cases and 12,462 controls) for functional relationships to genes in 16 known RA loci. They genotyped the 22 loci that scored significantly in 7,957 autoantibody-positive cases and 11,958 matched controls of European ancestry. Three new RA risk loci were confirmed at genomewide significance: rs11586238 on 1p13.1 near CD2 and CD58 (overall P = 1.0 x 10(-9)), rs1980422 on 2q33.2 near CD28 (overall P = 1.3 x 10(-9)), and rs548234 on 6q21 near PRDM1 (overall P = 2.1 x 10(-8)). Four more loci replicated but did not reach a conservative genomewide threshold: rs394581 near TAGAP on 6q25.3 (overall P = 3.8 x 10(-7)), rs10919563 in a PTPRC intron on 1q31.3 (overall P = 6.7 x 10(-7)), rs540386 in a TRAF6 intron on 11p12 (overall P = 3.9 x 10(-6)), and rs12746613 near FCGR2A on 1q23.3 (overall P = 1.5 x 10(-5)); the authors concluded that these likely represent true RA loci. The CD28 SNP rs1980422 lies 129 kb from the known risk allele rs3087243 in the CTLA4 region and is in minimal linkage disequilibrium with it, and conditional analysis confirmed that the 2 SNPs confer risk independently. There were no significant epistatic interactions among the 7 replicated SNPs and known RA risk alleles, and the 7 associations had consistent effects across all 14 collections. Several of the new loci lie near alleles associated with other autoimmune diseases, including FCGR2A (systemic lupus erythematosus), TAGAP (celiac disease and type 1 diabetes), PTPRC and CD58 (multiple sclerosis), and PRDM1 (Crohn disease), although none of the RA risk alleles corresponded perfectly to a previously established autoimmune allele.

paragraphs.text: In a genome-wide association study of common copy number variants (CNVs) in about 2,000 cases of each of 8 common diseases, including RA, and 3,000 shared controls, the Wellcome Trust Case Control Consortium et al. (2010) found CNVs in the HLA region associated with RA (CNVR2845.14, p = 1.4 x 10(-39); odds ratio, 1.77), but had no evidence that these were signals independent of the known associated HLA haplotypes. CNVR1065.1, annotated as mapping to chromosome 2, is actually a dispersed duplication with its polymorphism in the HLA region; it showed a strong signal in RA and type 1 diabetes and was well tagged by HLA SNPs known to be associated with both diseases. After correction for multiple testing, the multiallelic CNVs at CCL3L1, beta-defensin, and FCGR3A/B showed no significant association with RA, and the reported association between CCL3L1 and RA was not formally replicated (nominal p = 0.058).

paragraphs.text: Stahl et al. (2010) performed a GWAS meta-analysis of 5,539 autoantibody-positive RA cases and 20,169 controls of European descent, replicated the findings in 6,768 cases and 8,806 controls, and identified 7 new RA risk loci at genome-wide significance (P less than 5 x 10(-8)) in the combined analysis of 41,282 samples. Three loci had not been implicated in any earlier genetic study of RA or other autoimmune disease: 2p14 (rs934734, in intron 1 of SPRED2; P = 5.3 x 10(-10)), 5q11 (rs6859219, in ANKRD55 near IL6ST; P = 9.6 x 10(-12)), and 5q21 (rs26232, in C5orf30; P = 4.1 x 10(-8)). Loci already implicated in other autoimmune diseases were also associated with RA: 3p14 near PXK (rs13315591; P = 4.6 x 10(-8)), 4p15 near RBPJ (rs874040; P = 1.0 x 10(-16)), and 6q27 in CCR6 (rs3093023; P = 1.5 x 10(-11)); the IRF5 SNP rs10488631, chosen for its association with SLE, was also associated (P = 4.2 x 10(-11)). At IRF5, RA was associated with the group 1 SNP rs10488631 and the group 3 SNP rs4728142, whose effects were independent, but not with the group 2 SNP rs729302; the group 3 SNP rs3807306 was associated with autoantibody-positive RA (P = 4.5 x 10(-6)). At 2 known loci they found new alleles with effects at least partly independent of the previously implicated SNPs: CCL21 (rs951005; P = 3.9 x 10(-10)) and IL2RA (rs706778; P = 3.3 x 10(-11)). At IL2RA, RA risk was better explained by the rs2104286(T)-rs11594656(T) haplotype, which confers type 1 diabetes risk, than by rs706778. They also gave definitive evidence for association at AFF3 (rs11676922; P = 1.0 x 10(-14); odds ratio, 1.14). Eleven further SNPs, near IL6R, CD247, IL2/IL21, ZEB1, SH2B3, BATF, CD19/NFATC2IP, IKZF3, UBASH3A, and UBE2L3, replicated at P less than 0.05 without reaching genome-wide significance, and the authors suggested that most were likely genuine RA risk alleles.

paragraphs.text: Yen et al. (2001) found the KIR2DS2 gene in 83% of 30 Caucasian patients of Western European descent with rheumatoid vasculitis, compared with 39% of 70 RA patients without major organ involvement. This was a significant enrichment compared with normal controls (odds ratio, 5.56; P = 0.001) and with RA patients without vasculitis (odds ratio, 7.96; P = 0.001). KIR2DS2 was not more frequent in uncomplicated RA than in controls, so it did not affect the risk of RA itself. In logistic regression, KIR2DS2 conferred a risk of vasculitis independently of HLA-C*03. In CD4+CD28null T-cell clones from 3 patients with vasculitis, 58 to 91% of the clones expressed KIR2DS2, and cross-linking of CD158b costimulated IFN-gamma production.

paragraphs.text: Nedvetzki et al. (2003) found that synovial fluid cells from the joints of RA patients expressed a CD44 variant, designated CD44vRA, that encodes an extra trinucleotide (CAG) transcribed from intronic sequences flanking a variant exon. Namalwa cells transfected with CD44vRA bound the same amount of FGF2 as cells transfected with wildtype CD44v3-v10, but bound substantially more soluble FGFR1 and stimulated proliferation of FGFR1-bearing BaF-32 cells more efficiently.
